claim: Object classification has been proposed as a principal objective of the primate ventral visual stream.
source: Object classification has been proposed as a principal objective of the primate ventral visual stream and has been used as an optimization target for deep neural network models (DNNs) of the visual system.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Object classification has been used as an optimization target for deep neural network models (DNNs) of the visual system.
source: Object classification has been proposed as a principal objective of the primate ventral visual stream and has been used as an optimization target for deep neural network models (DNNs) of the visual system.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Visual brain areas represent many different types of information.
source: However, visual brain areas represent many different types of information, and optimizing for classification of object identity alone does not constrain how other information may be encoded in visual representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about visual brain areas.

claim: Optimizing for classification of object identity alone does not constrain how other information may be encoded in visual representations.
source: However, visual brain areas represent many different types of information, and optimizing for classification of object identity alone does not constrain how other information may be encoded in visual representations.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the limitations of single-objective optimization.

claim: Factorization of object pose and background information from object identity increased in higher-level regions of the monkey ventral visual hierarchy.
source: In the monkey ventral visual hierarchy, we found that factorization of object pose and background information from object identity increased in higher-level regions and strongly contributed to improving object identity decoding performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from monkey neural recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Factorization of object pose and background information from object identity strongly contributed to improving object identity decoding performance in the monkey ventral visual hierarchy.
source: In the monkey ventral visual hierarchy, we found that factorization of object pose and background information from object identity increased in higher-level regions and strongly contributed to improving object identity decoding performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from monkey neural recordings and decoding analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: DNN models which best matched neural, fMRI, and behavioral data from both monkeys and humans across 12 datasets tended to be those which factorized scene parameters most strongly.
source: Models which best matched neural, fMRI, and behavioral data from both monkeys and humans across 12 datasets tended to be those which factorized scene parameters most strongly.
evidence: This claim is supported by the large-scale analysis of DNN models presented in the manuscript.

claim: Invariance to scene parameters was not as consistently associated with matches to neural and behavioral data as factorization.
source: Notably, invariance to these parameters was not as consistently associated with matches to neural and behavioral data, suggesting that maintaining non-class information in factorized activity subspaces is often preferred to dropping it altogether.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis of factorization versus invariance metrics across multiple datasets.

claim: Maintaining non-class information in factorized activity subspaces is often preferred to dropping it altogether.
source: Notably, invariance to these parameters was not as consistently associated with matches to neural and behavioral data, suggesting that maintaining non-class information in factorized activity subspaces is often preferred to dropping it altogether.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing differential effects of factorization versus invariance.

claim: Factorization of visual scene information is a widely used strategy in brains and DNN models thereof.
source: Thus, we propose that factorization of visual scene information is a widely used strategy in brains and DNN models thereof.
evidence: This claim is based on the synthesis of findings from both neural data and DNN model analyses.

claim: DNNs trained to perform image classification produce internal feature representations broadly similar to those in areas V4 and IT of the primate cortex.
source: Many studies have reported that DNNs trained to perform image classification produce internal feature representations broadly similar to those in areas V4 and IT of the primate cortex, and that this similarity tends to be greater in models with better classification performance (Yamins et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work, specifically Yamins et al., 2014.

claim: The similarity between DNN representations and primate cortex representations tends to be greater in models with better classification performance.
source: Many studies have reported that DNNs trained to perform image classification produce internal feature representations broadly similar to those in areas V4 and IT of the primate cortex, and that this similarity tends to be greater in models with better classification performance (Yamins et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work, specifically Yamins et al., 2014.

claim: Beyond a certain threshold level of object classification performance, further improvement fails to produce a concomitant improvement in predicting primate neural responses.
source: Moreover, beyond a certain threshold level of object classification performance, further improvement fails to produce a concomitant improvement in predicting primate neural responses (Schrimpf et al., 2020; Nonaka et al., 2021; Linsley, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Schrimpf et al., 2020; Nonaka et al., 2021; Linsley, 2023).

claim: High-level cortical neurons in the primate ventral visual stream simultaneously encode many forms of information about visual input besides object identity, such as object pose.
source: However, high-level cortical neurons in the primate ventral visual stream are known to simultaneously encode many forms of information about visual input besides object identity, such as object pose (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Hong et al., 2016; Kravitz et al., 2013; Peters and Kriegeskorte, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Hong et al., 2016; Kravitz et al., 2013; Peters and Kriegeskorte, 2021).

claim: Factorization can enable simultaneous decoding of many parameters at once, supporting diverse visually guided behaviors.
source: Factorization can enable simultaneous decoding of many parameters at once, supporting diverse visually guided behaviors (e.g., spatial navigation, object manipulation, or object classification) (Johnston and Fusi, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Johnston and Fusi, 2023 and logical inference about the properties of factorized representations.

claim: Both V4 and IT responses exhibited more significant factorization of object identity information from non-identity information than a shuffle control.
source: We found that both V4 and IT responses exhibited more significant factorization of object identity information from non-identity information than a shuffle control (which accounts for effects on factorization due to dimensionality of these regions) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; see 'Methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from neural recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: The degree of factorization increased from V4 to IT.
source: Furthermore, the degree of factorization increased from V4 to IT (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Invariance to non-identity information increased from V4 to IT.
source: Consistent with prior studies, we also found that invariance to non-identity information increased from V4 to IT in our analysis (Figure 2A, right, solid lines; Rust and DiCarlo, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and citation to prior work (Rust and DiCarlo, 2010).

claim: Maintaining invariance alone in the neural population code was insufficient to account for a large fraction of decoding performance in high-level visual cortex.
source: Our analysis shows that maintaining invariance alone in the neural population code was insufficient to account for a large fraction of decoding performance in high-level visual cortex; factorization of non-identity variables is key to the decoding performance achieved by V4 and IT representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the lesion experiment data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Factorization of non-identity variables is key to the decoding performance achieved by V4 and IT representations.
source: Our analysis shows that maintaining invariance alone in the neural population code was insufficient to account for a large fraction of decoding performance in high-level visual cortex; factorization of non-identity variables is key to the decoding performance achieved by V4 and IT representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the lesion experiment data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The final layers of trained networks exhibited consistent increases in factorization of all tested scene parameters relative to a randomly initialized (untrained) baseline with the same architecture.
source: We found that the final layers of trained networks exhibited consistent increases in factorization of all tested scene parameters relative to a randomly initialized (untrained) baseline with the same architecture (Figure 4A, top row, rightward shift relative to black cross, a randomly initialized ResNet-50).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from DNN model analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Training DNNs produced mixed effects on invariance, typically increasing it for background and lighting but reducing it for object pose and camera viewpoint.
source: By contrast, training DNNs produced mixed effects on invariance, typically increasing it for background and lighting but reducing it for object pose and camera viewpoint (Figure 4A, bottom row, leftward shift relative to black cross for left two panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from DNN model analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The degree of factorization in models correlated with the degree to which they predicted neural activity for single-unit IT data.
source: Moreover, we found that the degree of factorization in models correlated with the degree to which they predicted neural activity for single-unit IT data (Figure 4A, top row), which can be seen as correlative evidence that neural representations in IT exhibit factorization of all scene variables tested.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between model factorization and neural predictivity shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Neural representations in IT exhibit factorization of all scene variables tested.
source: Moreover, we found that the degree of factorization in models correlated with the degree to which they predicted neural activity for single-unit IT data (Figure 4A, top row), which can be seen as correlative evidence that neural representations in IT exhibit factorization of all scene variables tested.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between model factorization and neural predictivity.

claim: IT neural representations build invariance to some scene information (background and lighting) but not to others (object pose and observer viewpoint).
source: Interestingly, we saw a different pattern for representational invariance to a scene parameter. Invariance showed mixed correlations with neural predictivity (Figure 4A, bottom row), suggesting that IT neural representations build invariance to some scene information (background and lighting) but not to others (object pose and observer viewpoint).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of correlations between model invariance and neural predictivity shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Increased factorization of scene parameters in model representations correlated with models being more predictive of neural spiking responses, voxel BOLD signal, and behavioral responses to images.
source: Consistently, increased factorization of scene parameters in model representations correlated with models being more predictive of neural spiking responses, voxel BOLD signal, and behavioral responses to images (Figure 5A, black bars; see Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3 for scatter plots across all datasets).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis across multiple datasets shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Invariance to appearance factors (background identity and scene lighting) correlated with more brainlike models.
source: Although invariance to appearance factors (background identity and scene lighting) correlated with more brainlike models, invariance for spatial transforms (object pose and camera viewpoint) consistently did not (zero or negative correlation values; Figure 5C, red and green open circles).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Invariance for spatial transforms (object pose and camera viewpoint) consistently did not correlate with more brainlike models.
source: Although invariance to appearance factors (background identity and scene lighting) correlated with more brainlike models, invariance for spatial transforms (object pose and camera viewpoint) consistently did not (zero or negative correlation values; Figure 5C, red and green open circles).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The main finding of a positive correlation between factorization and neural predictivity was robust to the particular choice of PCA threshold used to quantify factorization.
source: Furthermore, the main finding of a positive correlation between factorization and neural predictivity was robust to the particular choice of PCA threshold we used to quantify factorization (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Factorization scores significantly boosted cross-validated predictive power of neural/behavioral fit performance compared to simply using object classification alone.
source: However, we found that factorization scores significantly boosted cross-validated predictive power of neural/behavioral fit performance compared to simply using object classification alone, and factorization boosted predictive power as much if not slightly more when using RDMs instead of linear regression fits to quantify the match to the brain/behavior (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Considering factorization in addition to object classification performance improves upon our prior understanding of the properties of more brainlike models.
source: Thus, considering factorization in addition to object classification performance improves upon our prior understanding of the properties of more brainlike models (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Factorization is related to the existing concept of manifold disentanglement.
source: We note that our definition of factorization is closely related to the existing concept of manifold disentanglement (DiCarlo and Cox, 2007; Chung et al., 2018) and can be seen as a generalization of disentanglement to high-dimensional visual scene parameters like object pose.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on manifold disentanglement (DiCarlo and Cox, 2007; Chung et al., 2018).

claim: Factorization can be seen as a generalization of disentanglement to high-dimensional visual scene parameters like object pose.
source: We note that our definition of factorization is closely related to the existing concept of manifold disentanglement (DiCarlo and Cox, 2007; Chung et al., 2018) and can be seen as a generalization of disentanglement to high-dimensional visual scene parameters like object pose.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' conceptual framework relating factorization to disentanglement.

claim: The extent to which variables were represented in a factorized way influenced the ability of a linear discriminator to successfully decode both variables in a generalizable fashion from a few training samples.
source: In a simulation, we found that the extent to which the variables of interest were represented in a factorized way (i.e., along orthogonal axes, rather than correlated axes) influenced the ability of a linear discriminator to successfully decode both variables in a generalizable fashion from a few training samples (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A linear basis rotation that decreased factorization while leaving all other activity statistics intact had the effect of strongly reducing object identity decoding performance in both V4 and IT.
source: The applied linear basis rotation leaves all other activity statistics completely intact (such as mean neural firing rates, covariance structure of the population, and its invariance to non-class variables) yet has the effect of strongly reducing object identity decoding performance in both V4 and IT (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the lesion experiment data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Factorization of frame-by-frame variance from other sources of variance across natural movies was correlated with improved neural predictivity in both macaque and human data.
source: Similar to the result found for factorization measured using augmentations of synthetic images, factorization of frame-by-frame variance (local in time, presumably dominated by either observer or camera motion; see 'Methods') from other sources of variance across natural movies (non-local in time) was correlated with improved neural predictivity in both macaque and human data while invariance to local frame-by-frame differences was not (Figure 5B; black versus gray bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of natural movie data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Invariance to local frame-by-frame differences in natural movies was not correlated with improved neural predictivity.
source: Similar to the result found for factorization measured using augmentations of synthetic images, factorization of frame-by-frame variance (local in time, presumably dominated by either observer or camera motion; see 'Methods') from other sources of variance across natural movies (non-local in time) was correlated with improved neural predictivity in both macaque and human data while invariance to local frame-by-frame differences was not (Figure 5B; black versus gray bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of natural movie data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The relationship between factorization and matches to neural data was not entirely mediated by classification or dimensionality.
source: Critically, our results cannot be accounted for by classification performance or dimensionality alone (Figure 6, gray and pink bars); that is, the relationship between factorization and matches to neural data was not entirely mediated by classification or dimensionality.
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis controlling for classification and dimensionality shown in Figure 6.

claim: High-dimensional representations could be regarded as a means to facilitate factorization.
source: Indeed, high-dimensional representations could be regarded as a means to facilitate factorization, and likewise factorized representations can better support classification (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the relationship between dimensionality and factorization, supported by simulation data in Figure 1C.

claim: Factorized representations can better support classification.
source: Indeed, high-dimensional representations could be regarded as a means to facilitate factorization, and likewise factorized representations can better support classification (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the relationship between factorization and classification, supported by simulation data in Figure 1C.

claim: Machine learning models designed to infer disentangled representations of visual data displayed single-unit responses that resembled those of individual neurons in macaque IT.
source: One prior study notably found that machine learning models designed to infer disentangled representations of visual data displayed single-unit responses that resembled those of individual neurons in macaque IT (Higgins et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Higgins et al., 2021).

claim: A fully factorized representation should be highly abstract according to the definition of abstraction in representational geometry.
source: A fully factorized representation should be highly abstract according to this definition, though factorization emphasizes the geometric properties of the population representation while these studies emphasize the consequences for decoding performance in training downstream linear read-outs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the relationship between factorization and abstraction as defined in prior work.

claim: Orthogonal encoding of class and non-class information is one of several factors that determines few-shot classification performance.
source: Relatedly, another recent study found that orthogonal encoding of class and non-class information is one of several factors that determines few-shot classification performance (Sorscher et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Sorscher et al., 2022).

claim: Local straightening of natural movies was found to be important for early visual cortex neural responses but not necessarily for high-level visual cortex.
source: Local straightening of natural movies was found to be important for early visual cortex neural responses but not necessarily for high-level visual cortex (Toosi and Issa, 2022), where the present work suggests factorization may play a role.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Toosi and Issa, 2022).

claim: Factorization may play a role in high-level visual cortex.
source: Local straightening of natural movies was found to be important for early visual cortex neural responses but not necessarily for high-level visual cortex (Toosi and Issa, 2022), where the present work suggests factorization may play a role.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the findings of the present work.

claim: Factorization increases with higher dimensionality as this decreases overlap.
source: Intuitively, factorization increases with higher dimensionality as this decreases overlap, all other things being equal (in the limit, the angle between points will approach 90o or a fully orthogonal code in high dimensions), and for a given finite, fixed dimension, factorization is mainly driven by the angle between this dimension and the other variable subspaces which measures the degree of contamination (Figure 1C; square vs. parallelogram).
evidence: This claim is based on mathematical reasoning about high-dimensional spaces.

claim: In the limit of high dimensions, the angle between points will approach 90 degrees or a fully orthogonal code.
source: Intuitively, factorization increases with higher dimensionality as this decreases overlap, all other things being equal (in the limit, the angle between points will approach 90o or a fully orthogonal code in high dimensions), and for a given finite, fixed dimension, factorization is mainly driven by the angle between this dimension and the other variable subspaces which measures the degree of contamination (Figure 1C; square vs. parallelogram).
evidence: This claim is based on mathematical reasoning about high-dimensional spaces.

claim: For a given finite, fixed dimension, factorization is mainly driven by the angle between this dimension and the other variable subspaces which measures the degree of contamination.
source: Intuitively, factorization increases with higher dimensionality as this decreases overlap, all other things being equal (in the limit, the angle between points will approach 90o or a fully orthogonal code in high dimensions), and for a given finite, fixed dimension, factorization is mainly driven by the angle between this dimension and the other variable subspaces which measures the degree of contamination (Figure 1C; square vs. parallelogram).
evidence: This claim is based on mathematical reasoning about the geometry of factorization.

claim: Invariance to non-identity information was more pronounced when measured in the subspace of population activity capturing the bulk (90%) of identity-driven variance as a consequence of increased factorization of identity from non-identity information.
source: Invariance to non-identity information was even more pronounced when measured in the subspace of population activity capturing the bulk (90%) of identity-driven variance as a consequence of increased factorization of identity from non-identity information (Figure 2A, right, dashed lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The normalized factorization scores remained significantly above zero for both V4 and IT brain areas after subtracting shuffle control.
source: Shuffling the image identities of each population vector accounts for increases in factorization driven purely by changes in the covariance statistics of population responses between V4 and IT. However, the normalized factorization scores remained significantly above zero for both brain areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The results were preserved when re-running the analyses using only the subset of models with the identical ResNet-50 architecture.
source: Our results were preserved when we re-ran the analyses using only the subset of models with the identical ResNet-50 architecture (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) or when we evaluated model predictivity using representational dissimilarity matrices of the population (RDMs) instead of linear regression (encoding) fits of individual neurons or voxels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by control analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The results were preserved when evaluating model predictivity using representational dissimilarity matrices of the population (RDMs) instead of linear regression (encoding) fits of individual neurons or voxels.
source: Our results were preserved when we re-ran the analyses using only the subset of models with the identical ResNet-50 architecture (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) or when we evaluated model predictivity using representational dissimilarity matrices of the population (RDMs) instead of linear regression (encoding) fits of individual neurons or voxels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by control analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Similar results were found using a covariance-based method for computing factorization that does not have any free parameters.
source: We found similar results using a covariance-based method for computing factorization that does not have any free parameters (Figure 5C, faded filled circles; see Equations 4 in 'Methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of two methods shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Factorization of non-class information is an important strategy used, alongside invariance, by the high-level visual cortex.
source: Here, we presented evidence that factorization of non-class information is an important strategy used, alongside invariance, by the high-level visual cortex (Figure 2) and by DNNs that are predictive of primate neural and behavioral data (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from neural recordings and DNN model analyses.

claim: Factorization of non-class information is an important strategy used by DNNs that are predictive of primate neural and behavioral data.
source: Here, we presented evidence that factorization of non-class information is an important strategy used, alongside invariance, by the high-level visual cortex (Figure 2) and by DNNs that are predictive of primate neural and behavioral data (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNN model analyses shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Building representations that support object classification performance and representations that preserve high-dimensional information about natural images are both important principles of the primate visual system.
source: Prior work has indicated that building representations that support object classification performance and representations that preserve high-dimensional information about natural images are both important principles of the primate visual system (Cadieu et al., 2014; Elmoznino and Bonner, 2022; though see Conwell et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Cadieu et al., 2014; Elmoznino and Bonner, 2022; Conwell et al., 2022).

claim: Artificial deep neural networks (DNNs) are the most predictive models of neural responses to images in the primate high-level visual cortex.
source: Artificial deep neural networks (DNNs) are the most predictive models of neural responses to images in the primate high-level visual cortex (Cadieu et al., 2014; Schrimpf et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Cadieu et al., 2014; Schrimpf et al., 2020).
